claims.text: A continuous protective oxide scale governs oxidation resistance and material integrity in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys.
Surface segregation of oxidation-resistant elements is primarily responsible for development of the protective oxide scale.
Al segregation can produce a predominantly Al2O3 protective scale.
The proposed initial alloy is homogeneous and contains uniformly distributed Al and other oxidizable elements.
At high temperature under oxidizing conditions, selected elements such as Al preferentially diffuse to the alloy surface.
The surface-enriched elements oxidize to form a protective layer.
The protective oxide layer limits subsequent oxygen ingress.
Protective-scale formation depends on the intrinsic diffusivity of the scale-forming element.
Alloy processing history can enhance elemental segregation.
Greater surface segregation of oxidation-resistant elements will produce a more uniform and continuous oxide scale.
Greater surface segregation will lower oxidation rates relative to an otherwise identical alloy with less segregation.
Lower oxidation rates will be observable as lower weight gain and more stable scale morphology.
An alloy processed without segregation-promoting pretreatment will develop a less effective or patchier oxide scale under identical oxidation conditions.
The segregation-controlled mechanism should dominate during sustained high-temperature exposure up to approximately 1100°C, where diffusion is active.
At lower temperatures, other kinetic limitations may mask the effect of segregation.
The effect of pre-induced segregation on oxide-scale uniformity in multiprincipal-element alloys has not been thoroughly documented in time-resolved studies.

Failure of segregation-promoting pretreatment to yield a statistically significant improvement in scale uniformity, continuity, integrity, and oxidation weight gain relative to the as-cast control would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
